newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee ends dull session weaker, awaits ACPC.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee ends dull session weaker, awaits ACPC.

text.p: CSCE coffee prices pulled back slightly in scant turnover Thursday, as traders awaited news from producers' talks scheduled to begin tomorrow in London.
Light speculative selling kept prices under pressure throughout the session, but participation from commercial houses was limited, dealers said.
Benchmark December futures slipped 0.75 cent per lb, to 105.70, having traded from 105.15 to 106.60. The day's volume was estimated at a paltry 3,877 lots.

Traders said December's ability to hold above key chart support levels at 104.50 and 101.50 cents strengthened the market's tone, but they warned that the market could stage a rapid retreat if it continually failed to make new highs.

"As long as December is above 104.50 cents, technically the market should try to creep higher," said Victor Henriquez, president of the trading firm Hencorp Becstone. "But the market has no momentum."
Some traders said the market appeared to be biding its time ahead of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) meeting, scheduled for Friday and Saturday.
While no major policy changes are anticipated at the meeting, dealers said uncertainty over the ACPC's intentions dampened market interest.
The producers' cartel was expected to review its current export quota scheme, which currently limits exports by its 14 members to 53.5 million 60-kg bags in the year to June 1997.

Since the ACPC renewed its commitment to export restrictions last May, New York futures prices have see-sawed within a 30-cent range. But producers, worried that the arrival of the 1996/97 harvest will send prices spiralling downward, might take steps to reaffirm their commitment to sales restrictions.

Market participants were also keeping their eye on Colombia, where recent attacks by rebels has blocked some highways and caused delays to shipments, industry officials said. Colombia is the world's second biggest coffee grower.
But traders were reluctant to bid the market higher on the news, choosing instead to see if the Samper government was able to put down the insurrection before the main-crop harvest begins next month.
"Traders are not going to rush to buy because something might happen," Henriquez said. "That's the lesson they have learned in the last two years. They're just going to buy coffee when they need it."
-- Wendy Pollack, New York Commodities Desk +1 212 859 1640
